title: The 30-Minute Friday Decision Review: A Simple Ritual That Makes Founders Better Decision-Makers

children: The Friday Decision Review: 30 minutes, once a week.
68% of owners delayed or avoided a major decision this year. Here's a weekly template for founders who make too many calls alone and too few on purpose.
Most founders don't have a decision problem. Instead, they have a decision
backlog
: dozens of choices made on the fly, a few big ones postponed for months, and no time set aside to look at either.

That backlog is more common, and more expensive, than most owners realize. This article shares the data behind it and a simple ritual that fixes it in 30 minutes a week. No software needed; a notebook works.
The decision backlog, by the numbers
Bluevine's 2026 survey of 781 small business owners found something striking.
Stress freezes decisions
68% delayed or avoided a major business decision
in the past 12 months because of financial stress: hiring, buying equipment, expanding.
report moderate to extremely high financial stress.
delayed big decisions repeatedly or on a regular basis.
In other words, two out of three owners have at least one important decision sitting in limbo. And Patriot Software's 2026 research shows the toll that takes:
53.5% of owners lose sleep over their business at least a few times a week.
Undecided decisions don't stay quiet. They replay at night, drain energy during the day and quietly cost money while they wait.
Why founders postpone decisions
It's rarely laziness. Usually, it's one of these:
Fear of being wrong
in front of the team, investors or family.
Missing information,
or the belief that more information will make the choice easier.
No one to talk it through with,
so the decision loops in one head.
No deadline,
so there's always a reason to wait until next week.
Too many small decisions,
crowding out the big ones.
The ritual below addresses each of these directly.
The ritual at a glance
The four parts and how long each one takes.
Pick a fixed slot, ideally Friday afternoon when the week is still fresh. Close email. Set a timer. The ritual has four parts: review, name, date and stop.
Part 1: Review last week's calls (10 minutes)
List the five most important decisions you made this week. For each, write one line:
What did I decide?
What did I expect to happen?
What actually happened so far?
The point isn't to judge yourself. Rather, it's to notice patterns. Over a few weeks you'll see them: you hire too fast, you discount too easily, you say yes to customers you should decline.
This is also how founders get better at deciding. Without a record, every decision feels new. With one, you build a personal database of what works for you.
Part 2: Name the decision you're avoiding (5 minutes)
Every founder has one. A conversation with a partner, a price increase, a person who isn't working out, a lease, a loan.
Write it down in one sentence. Then answer two questions:
What is waiting costing me each week?
What information am I actually missing?
Frequently, the honest answer to the second question is "nothing." In that case, the decision isn't blocked by information; it's blocked by discomfort.
If you're not missing any information, the decision isn't blocked by information. It's blocked by discomfort.
Naming that is powerful. Discomfort can be managed: by talking to someone, by shrinking the decision or by setting a date.
Part 3: Set decision dates (10 minutes)
For each open decision, assign:
A decision date.
When you'll decide regardless.
The smallest reversible version.
Can you test it instead of committing fully?
One outside opinion.
Who has faced this before and could pressure-test it?
Consequently, open loops become scheduled decisions, and your mind stops replaying them at night.

The "smallest reversible version" is especially useful. Instead of "hire a salesperson," try "hire a contractor for 90 days." Instead of "raise all prices," try "raise prices for new customers this month." Reversible tests turn scary decisions into experiments.
Part 4: Choose one thing to stop (5 minutes)
Founders add tasks constantly but rarely remove any. Therefore, end the review by choosing one recurring thing to stop, delegate or automate next week.
Over a year, that's 50 things off your plate. That's how founders create time for the decisions that matter.
Why this works
Decisions made alone go wrong three ways. The ritual fixes all three.

Decisions made alone tend to be delayed, distorted or hidden. This ritual counters all three: it puts deadlines on delay, adds outside input to distortion, and makes your reasoning visible, even if only to yourself.
It also works because it's small. Thirty minutes is easy to protect. And because it happens every week, nothing important sits for more than seven days without being looked at.
A worked example
Here's what a real Friday review might look like for the owner of a 12-person marketing agency.
Part 1, last week's calls:

Agreed to a 15% discount for a new client (expected: win the deal; actual: won it, but scope is already creeping). Hired a freelance designer (expected: faster turnaround; actual: too early to tell). Declined a speaking event (expected: more time; actual: used the time on proposals). The pattern after a few weeks: discounts keep leading to scope creep.
Part 2, the avoided decision:
"Should we let go of our longest-standing client, who's now unprofitable?" Cost of waiting: about $3,000 a month in unbilled hours and a frustrated team. Missing information: honestly, none.
Part 3, decision dates:

Decide by the end of the month. Smallest reversible version: propose a repriced scope first and let the client choose. Outside opinion: ask two agency founders in the peer group who've repriced legacy clients.
Part 4, one thing to stop:
Stop attending the weekly status call for a client the account manager already handles.
Thirty minutes. One avoided decision now has a date, a test and two advisors. One recurring task is gone. Multiply that by 52 weeks.
Common mistakes with the ritual
Turning it into a to-do list review.
This is about decisions, not tasks.
Skipping Part 2 when it's uncomfortable.
That's precisely when it matters most.
Setting dates and ignoring them.
If a date passes, the next review should ask why.
Doing it only when things are bad.
The habit is most valuable when it's consistent.
Making it stick
A few tips from founders who've kept this habit for months:
Put it in the calendar as a recurring meeting with yourself,
and treat it like a client meeting.
Use the same notebook or document every week,
so you can look back.
Start small.
If 30 minutes feels like too much, do 15 and grow from there.
Review monthly.
Once a month, read your last four reviews. Patterns jump out.
Do it with someone.
A peer founder, a coach or a group makes it far more effective.
Even better: do Part 3 with other founders
The outside opinion in Part 3 is where most founders get stuck. It's easy to say "ask someone who's faced this." It's harder to actually have that person available on a Friday afternoon.

Frequently asked questions
What is a weekly decision review?
A 30-minute ritual to review last week's key decisions, name the one you're avoiding, set decision dates and choose one thing to stop.
How common is decision avoidance among business owners?
Very common. Bluevine's 2026 survey found 68% of owners delayed or avoided a major business decision in the past year due to financial stress.
Why do founders avoid decisions?
Often not for lack of information, but because the decision is uncomfortable and there's nobody to pressure-test it with.
How do I make a hard decision faster?
Shrink it into a reversible test, set a date and get one outside opinion from someone who has faced it.
